title: Agentic Workflows
description: How AI agents plan, use tools, manage memory, and chain actions. ReAct, CoT, and agent orchestration patterns.

data.text: An AI agent is a system that uses an LLM as its reasoning engine to autonomously plan, act, observe results, and iterate until a goal is met. Unlike a simple chatbot that responds to one message, an agent operates in a loop — deciding what to do, executing actions through tools, reflecting on the outcome, and adjusting its strategy. This loop is what makes agents powerful for complex, multi-step tasks.

Every agent, regardless of its specific design, follows some form of the observe-think-act-reflect loop. The agent receives input, reasons about what to do next using the LLM, executes an action (usually by calling a tool or API), observes the result, and feeds that result back into its reasoning for the next step.

data.text: ReAct (Reason + Act) is one of the most influential agent prompting patterns. Instead of asking the LLM to either think or act, ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with actions in a structured format: Thought → Action → Observation → Thought → Action → Observation... This makes the agent's reasoning explicit, traceable, and easier to debug.

data.title: ReAct trace example
data.content:
Question: What is the elevation of the highest peak in the country whose president won the 2023 election in Turkey?

Thought 1: I need to find which country's president won the 2023 election in Turkey.
Action 1: Search[2023 Turkey presidential election winner]
Observation 1: Recep Tayyip Erdoğan won the 2023 Turkish presidential election. He is the president of Turkey.

Thought 2: So the country is Turkey. Now I need the highest peak in Turkey and its elevation.
Action 2: Search[highest peak in Turkey elevation]
Observation 2: Mount Ararat is the highest peak in Turkey at 5,137 meters.

Thought 3: I have all the information needed.
Action 3: Finish[The highest peak in Turkey is Mount Ararat at 5,137 meters]

data.text: Effective agents don't just react — they plan. Task decomposition breaks complex goals into smaller, manageable sub-tasks. Modern agents use techniques like chain-of-thought prompting to generate step-by-step plans, and tree-of-thought to explore alternative plans before committing to one.

data.title: Planning techniques:
items: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) — generate a linear sequence of reasoning steps
Tree-of-Thought (ToT) — explore multiple reasoning branches and select the best path
Graph-of-Thought (GoT) — allow arbitrary connections between reasoning steps for complex problems
LLM-as-Planner — use a separate LLM call to generate a full plan before execution
Reflexion — after completing a task, reflect on what went wrong and generate feedback for future attempts

data.text: Tools are the bridge between an LLM's reasoning and the real world. Modern agent frameworks support structured function calling, where the LLM outputs a machine-readable function call instead of free text. The framework then executes the function and feeds the result back. This enables reliable, type-safe interaction with APIs, databases, and external services.

Function calling is what makes agents reliable. Instead of parsing free-form text to figure out what the agent wants to do, you give the LLM a strict schema of available tools and let it output structured calls. This eliminates most parsing errors.

Agents need memory to maintain context across multiple steps and sessions. There are three main types of memory: working memory (the current conversation context), episodic memory (records of past interactions and their outcomes), and semantic memory (persistent knowledge about the world, like user preferences or domain facts).

data.text: When a task is too complex for a single agent, multiple agents can be orchestrated together. Orchestration patterns include sequential pipelines (agent A's output feeds agent B), parallel fan-out (multiple agents work simultaneously), hierarchical managers (a coordinator delegates to specialists), and swarm coordination (agents communicate peer-to-peer).

data.title: The orchestration tax
data.text: Each handoff between agents adds latency, cost, and potential for error. More agents don't automatically mean better results. Start with one capable agent, measure its failures, and add specialization only where it clearly helps.

Evaluating agents is harder than evaluating single-prompt LLMs because agent behavior is non-deterministic and multi-step. Key metrics include task success rate, average steps to completion, tool-call accuracy, and human-judged helpfulness. Frameworks like LangSmith and Phoenix provide tracing and evaluation specifically designed for agent workflows.

terms.definition: A prompting pattern that interleaves reasoning traces (Thought) with actions (Action) and observations (Observation).
A structured interface where the LLM outputs a machine-readable function call instead of free text.
The short-term context available to an agent during its current task, typically bounded by the LLM's context window.

data.title: Summary
points: Agents use an LLM as a reasoning engine in an observe-think-act loop
ReAct interleaves reasoning and actions for traceable, debuggable agent behavior
Planning breaks complex goals into executable sub-tasks
Function calling enables type-safe, reliable tool use
Memory systems preserve context across steps and sessions
Orchestration combines multiple agents for complex workflows
Agent evaluation must measure multi-step success, not just single-turn accuracy
data.takeaway: Agents extend LLMs from passive responders to active problem-solvers by adding planning, tools, and iterative loops.
